lesson.title: Cloud Computing and Azure Global Infrastructure
objectives: Explain cloud computing and the CapEx-to-OpEx shift in plain terms.
Compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and apply the shared responsibility model.
Describe Azure geographies, regions, region pairs and availability zones.
Choose a region using latency, compliance, service availability and price.
Answer the opening questions of an Azure administrator interview with confidence.
lesson.definition: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, networking and software over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's public cloud: a global network of datacentres grouped into regions, on which you create resources through a single management layer instead of buying and racking your own hardware.

theory.heading: Why organisations move to the cloud
theory.body: On-premises IT requires large up-front capital expenditure (CapEx) on servers, storage and datacentre space that must be sized for peak demand and then sits idle most of the time. The cloud converts this into operational expenditure (OpEx): you pay for what you consume, scale up for a festival sale and scale back down the next day. Administrators care about this because it changes their job from replacing failed disks to designing for elasticity, governance and cost control.
points: High availability: services are designed to keep running despite component failures.
Scalability and elasticity: add or remove capacity manually (scale) or automatically (elastic).
Agility: provision a VM or database in minutes, not weeks.
Global reach: deploy close to users in many countries.
Consumption-based pricing: no idle hardware bill, but you must watch for waste.

theory.heading: Service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
theory.body: The service model decides how much of the stack you manage. In IaaS (Azure Virtual Machines) you manage the operating system, patching, runtime and application while Microsoft manages the physical host. In PaaS (App Service, Azure SQL Database) Microsoft also manages the OS and runtime, so you focus on code, configuration and data. In SaaS (Microsoft 365) you only consume the application and manage your data, users and devices.
points: IaaS: most control, most responsibility (VMs, managed disks, virtual networks).
PaaS: platform handles OS patching and scaling plumbing (App Service, Azure SQL, Functions).
SaaS: finished software delivered over the internet (Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365).
Serverless (Functions, Logic Apps) is a PaaS style billed per execution.

theory.heading: The shared responsibility model
theory.body: Security and operations are split between Microsoft and the customer. Microsoft always owns physical datacentres, hosts and the physical network. The customer always owns their data, endpoints (devices) and accounts and identities, in every model. Everything in between moves from the customer towards Microsoft as you go from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS. This is why a breached password is always the customer's problem, even on SaaS.
points: Always customer: information and data, devices, accounts and identities.
Always Microsoft: physical hosts, physical network, physical datacentre.
Operating system: customer in IaaS, Microsoft in PaaS and SaaS.
Applications and network controls: customer in IaaS, shared in PaaS, Microsoft in SaaS.
Identity and directory infrastructure: customer in IaaS, shared in PaaS and SaaS.

theory.heading: Azure global infrastructure
theory.body: A region is a set of datacentres within a latency-defined perimeter, such as Central India (Pune) or South India (Chennai). Regions are grouped into geographies that respect data-residency and compliance boundaries. Many regions have a paired region in the same geography; Azure staggers platform updates across pairs and prioritises recovery of one region in each pair during a wide outage. Availability zones are physically separate datacentres (independent power, cooling and networking) inside one region, normally three per supported region.
points: Region: where your resource physically runs; choose it per resource.
Availability zone: protects against a datacentre failure inside a region.
Region pair: protects against a whole-region disaster; used by GRS storage replication.
Sovereign clouds (Azure Government, Azure operated by 21Vianet in China) are isolated instances.
Not every service or VM size is available in every region; check before designing.

theory.heading: Choosing a region
theory.body: Interviewers often ask how you would pick a region. A strong answer weighs four factors in order: compliance and data residency (Indian banking data may need to stay in India), latency to users, availability of the required services and zones, and price, which varies between regions for the same VM size.
points: Compliance first: some data must not leave the country.
Latency: put workloads near users; test with tools such as Azure speed tests.
Capability: zones, specific VM series or services may be missing in smaller regions.
Cost: the same SKU can cost noticeably more in one region than another.

example.title: Listing regions and zone support with Azure CLI
example.body: Before choosing where to deploy, an administrator checks which regions exist and which VM sizes support zones in a region. The CLI queries Azure Resource Manager, so the answer reflects your subscription's actual access.

code.source:
# All regions available to the subscription
az account list-locations --query "[].{name:name, display:displayName, pair:metadata.pairedRegion[0].name}" -o table

# Which zones a VM size supports in Central India
az vm list-skus --location centralindia --size Standard_D2s_v5 --zone -o table

demonstration.description: Map common tasks to the party responsible under each service model. This is the reasoning interviewers want when they ask 'who patches the OS on App Service?'.

code.source:
Task                         IaaS (VM)   PaaS (App Service)   SaaS (Microsoft 365)
Patch the guest OS           Customer    Microsoft            Microsoft
Configure app network rules  Customer    Shared               Microsoft

demonstration.output: Data, devices and identities stay with the customer in every model; physical infrastructure stays with Microsoft; the OS moves to Microsoft as soon as you use PaaS.

takeaways: Cloud turns up-front CapEx into consumption-based OpEx and adds elasticity.
IaaS gives most control and most responsibility; SaaS gives the least of both.
Data, devices and identities are always the customer's responsibility.
Availability zones protect against datacentre failure; region pairs protect against regional disasters.
Pick regions by compliance, latency, service availability and price, in that order.
Not every VM size or service exists in every region.

interview.question: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS? Give an Azure example of each.
interview.answer: IaaS provides virtual infrastructure where you manage the OS and above, for example Azure Virtual Machines. PaaS provides a managed platform where you deploy code and data, for example Azure App Service or Azure SQL Database. SaaS is complete software you consume, for example Microsoft 365.
interview.explanation: A strong answer ties each model to who patches the operating system, which shows you understand the operational consequence, not just the acronym.

interview.question: Explain the shared responsibility model.
interview.answer: Security duties are split between the cloud provider and the customer. Microsoft always secures the physical datacentre, hosts and network. The customer always owns data, devices and identities. Responsibility for the OS, network controls and applications shifts towards Microsoft as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS.
interview.explanation: Mention the 'always customer' items explicitly; many candidates wrongly say SaaS makes Microsoft responsible for everything.

interview.question: What is the difference between a region, an availability zone and a region pair?
interview.answer: A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacentres. An availability zone is a physically separate datacentre group inside a region with independent power, cooling and network. A region pair links two regions in the same geography for disaster recovery, staggered updates and prioritised recovery.
interview.explanation: Link each to the failure it protects against: zone for a datacentre failure, pair for a regional disaster.

interview.question: How would you choose an Azure region for a new workload?
interview.answer: First confirm compliance and data-residency requirements, then pick the region with the lowest latency to users that offers the required services, VM sizes and availability zones, and finally compare price between the shortlisted regions.
interview.explanation: Ordering the factors shows judgement; compliance is a hard constraint while price is a trade-off.

interview.question: What is the difference between scalability and elasticity?
interview.answer: Scalability is the ability to add capacity, either vertically (a bigger VM) or horizontally (more instances). Elasticity is scaling automatically in both directions in response to demand, such as autoscale rules on a scale set.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like the vertical versus horizontal distinction and a concrete Azure feature for elasticity.

practice.title: Shared responsibility lookup
practice.objective: Encode the Azure shared responsibility model and use it to answer 'who owns this?' questions for any service model.
practice.statement: Read a service model (IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, case-insensitive) and a list of responsibility layers. For each layer print who is responsible: Customer, Microsoft or Shared. Use this model: data, devices and accounts are always Customer; physical is always Microsoft; os is Customer for IaaS and Microsoft otherwise; applications and network are Customer for IaaS, Shared for PaaS and Microsoft for SaaS; identity is Customer for IaaS and Shared for PaaS and SaaS. Any other layer name prints Unknown. If the model itself is not one of the three, print only 'Invalid model'.
practice.input_format: Line 1: the service model. Line 2: N, the number of layers. Next N lines: one layer name each (case-insensitive).
practice.output_format: For each layer, one line '<layer>: <owner>' with the layer in lowercase, or a single line 'Invalid model'.

data: Customer
network: Shared

constraints: Layer names are compared in lowercase.

n = int(input())

    'devices': ('Customer', 'Customer', 'Customer'),
    'accounts': ('Customer', 'Customer', 'Customer'),
    'identity': ('Customer', 'Shared', 'Shared'),
    'applications': ('Customer', 'Shared', 'Microsoft'),
    'network': ('Customer', 'Shared', 'Microsoft'),
    'os': ('Customer', 'Microsoft', 'Microsoft'),

Map the service model to a column index; reject anything else with 'Invalid model'.

lesson.title: Azure Resource Manager: Management Groups, Subscriptions and Resource Groups
objectives: Explain what Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is and why every tool goes through it.
Describe the four-level hierarchy: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources.
Decide when to create a new subscription versus a new resource group.
Create and organise resource groups with Azure CLI and PowerShell.
Explain how settings applied at a higher scope are inherited by lower scopes.
lesson.definition: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service for Azure: every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs or templates is authenticated, authorised and then sent by ARM to the right resource provider. ARM organises resources in a hierarchy of management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources, and access control, policy and budgets applied at one level are inherited by everything beneath it.

theory.heading: What Azure Resource Manager does
theory.body: ARM is the single control plane in front of all Azure services. When you run 'az vm create', the CLI calls the ARM REST API; ARM checks your identity with Microsoft Entra ID, checks RBAC permissions, evaluates Azure Policy, and only then forwards the request to the Microsoft.Compute resource provider. Because every tool uses the same API, results are consistent and you can describe infrastructure declaratively with ARM templates or Bicep.
points: Control plane (management.azure.com): create, update, delete and configure resources.
Data plane: using the resource itself, such as reading a blob or connecting to a VM.
Resource providers (Microsoft.Compute, Microsoft.Storage, Microsoft.Network) must be registered in a subscription.
Resource ID format: /subscriptions/{id}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/{namespace}/{type}/{name}.

theory.heading: The management hierarchy
theory.body: Management groups sit at the top and contain subscriptions or other management groups. Every Microsoft Entra tenant has one Tenant Root Group. Below management groups are subscriptions, then resource groups, then resources. The hierarchy exists so that governance (RBAC, Azure Policy) can be applied once at a high level and flow down automatically, instead of being configured on thousands of resources.
points: Management groups: up to six levels of depth below the root (root and subscription levels not counted).
Each management group or subscription has exactly one parent.
Subscription: a billing, quota and access boundary, trusted by exactly one Entra tenant.
Resource group: a logical container for resources that share a lifecycle.
Resource: an individual VM, storage account, VNet, database and so on.

theory.heading: Subscriptions as boundaries
theory.body: A subscription is where usage is billed and where many quotas (for example vCPUs per region) are enforced. Organisations create separate subscriptions to separate billing (one per department or customer), to separate environments (production and development), to isolate access, or simply because one subscription would hit a scale limit. Subscriptions are grouped under management groups such as Platform, Landing Zones and Sandbox in the Azure landing zone model.
points: Billing boundary: invoices and cost reports are produced per subscription.
Access boundary: owners of one subscription have no rights in another by default.
Quota boundary: request vCPU quota increases per subscription and region.
A subscription can be moved to a different tenant, but RBAC assignments in it are lost.

theory.heading: Resource groups
theory.body: A resource group holds resources that are deployed, managed and deleted together, such as the VMs, disks and network interface of one application. A resource group has a location, but that only stores its metadata; the resources inside can live in other regions. Resource groups cannot be nested, and a resource belongs to exactly one resource group at a time, although most resources can be moved between groups and subscriptions.
points: Group by lifecycle: if things are created and deleted together, keep them together.
Deleting a resource group deletes every resource in it, so use locks on production.
Moving a resource changes its resource ID, so scripts and alerts referring to it must be updated.
Use a naming convention such as rg-<app>-<env>-<region>.

theory.heading: Inheritance and scope
theory.body: A scope is any level of the hierarchy at which you can assign roles, policies, locks or budgets. Assignments flow downward: a Reader role granted on a management group gives read access to every subscription, resource group and resource beneath it. This is why governance teams build management group structures first and why you should avoid granting broad roles at high scopes.
points: Scope order from broad to narrow: management group, subscription, resource group, resource.
Lower scopes cannot remove rights granted higher up (except deny assignments).
Policies at a management group apply to all current and future subscriptions inside it.

example.title: Building a small hierarchy with Azure CLI
example.body: A governance team creates a management group for production, moves a subscription into it and creates a resource group for a web application. The resource group metadata lives in Central India.

code.source:
az account management-group create --name mg-prod --display-name "Production"
az account management-group subscription add --name mg-prod --subscription "Contoso-Prod"

az account set --subscription "Contoso-Prod"
az group create --name rg-shop-prod-cin --location centralindia --tags env=prod app=shop
az group list --query "[].{name:name, location:location}" -o table

takeaways: Every Azure tool talks to Azure Resource Manager, which authenticates, authorises and applies policy.
Hierarchy: management groups > subscriptions > resource groups > resources.
Management groups support six levels of depth below the Tenant Root Group.
A subscription is a billing, quota and access boundary trusted by one Entra tenant.
Resource groups group by lifecycle; their location stores metadata only.
Assignments at a higher scope are inherited by every lower scope.

interview.question: What is Azure Resource Manager?
interview.answer: ARM is Azure's management layer. All requests from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs and templates go through it; it authenticates the caller, checks RBAC and policy and forwards the request to the resource provider.
interview.explanation: Mention that this is why behaviour is consistent across tools and why templates can be declarative.

interview.question: When would you create a new subscription instead of a new resource group?
interview.answer: When you need a separate billing boundary, a strong access or environment boundary such as production versus development, separate quotas, or when an existing subscription is reaching scale limits. Resource groups are for grouping resources with the same lifecycle within a subscription.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want the boundary concept: subscriptions separate billing, access and quota; resource groups separate lifecycle.

interview.question: Can a resource group contain resources from different regions?
interview.answer: Yes. The resource group's location only stores its metadata. Resources inside can be in any region, although keeping metadata in a compliant region matters for some regulations.
interview.explanation: A common trick question. Mention the metadata point and the compliance nuance.

interview.question: What are management groups and why use them?
interview.answer: Management groups are containers above subscriptions. Policies and role assignments applied to a management group are inherited by all subscriptions beneath it, so governance is applied once for many subscriptions. They support up to six levels of depth under the Tenant Root Group.
interview.explanation: A strong answer gives an example structure (Platform, Landing Zones, Sandbox) and mentions inheritance.

interview.question: What happens when you move a resource to another resource group or subscription?
interview.answer: Both source and target groups are locked for writes during the move, and the resource gets a new resource ID. Not all resource types support moving, some have dependencies that must move together, and RBAC assignments made directly on the resource do not move with it.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the ID change and the need to update scripts, alerts and role assignments shows real operational experience.

quiz.question: Which component authenticates and authorises every Azure management request before it reaches a resource provider?
quiz.explanation: ARM is the control plane that every tool calls; it authenticates with Entra ID, checks RBAC and policy and then forwards the request.

quiz.question: You create a resource group in Central India. Can you deploy a storage account in South India into that resource group?
options: Only if the regions are a region pair
Only after enabling cross-region resource groups
Yes, the resource group location only stores metadata
No, resources must match the resource group region
quiz.explanation: Resources in a group can be in any region; the group's location is where its metadata is stored.

quiz.question: How many levels of management group depth are supported below the Tenant Root Group (not counting the root or subscription levels)?
quiz.explanation: A management group tree supports up to six levels of depth, excluding the root level and the subscription level.

quiz.question: Finance wants a separate invoice and separate vCPU quotas for the analytics department. What should you create?
quiz.explanation: Subscriptions are billing and quota boundaries. Resource groups and tags do not create separate quotas.

quiz.question: A VM is moved from rg-old to rg-new in the same subscription. What must you expect?
options: The VM is redeployed and its disks are recreated
The VM keeps the same resource ID
The VM's resource ID changes, so references to the old ID must be updated
The move automatically copies all role assignments
quiz.explanation: The resource group is part of the resource ID, so the ID changes. Role assignments made directly on the resource are not carried over.

lesson.title: Tags and Resource Locks for Organising and Protecting Resources
objectives: Design a tagging strategy for cost reporting, ownership and automation.
Explain why tags are not inherited and how to enforce or inherit them with Azure Policy.
Compare CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks and predict which operations each blocks.
Explain lock inheritance and who is allowed to create or remove locks.
Recognise the side effects of ReadOnly locks on real services.
lesson.definition: Tags are name-value pairs attached to Azure resources, resource groups and subscriptions to add metadata such as cost centre, environment or owner. Resource locks are management-plane safeguards that prevent accidental deletion (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly) to a scope and everything beneath it, regardless of the user's RBAC role.

theory.heading: Why tags matter
theory.body: In a large estate, resource names alone cannot answer 'who owns this VM?' or 'how much does the payroll project cost?'. Tags carry that metadata. Cost Management can group and filter spend by tag, automation can shut down every VM tagged autoshutdown=true at 8 pm, and operations teams can find the owner of an alerting resource in seconds.
points: Common tags: env, costCenter, owner, app, dataClassification.
Up to 50 tag name-value pairs per resource, resource group or subscription.
Tag names are case-insensitive for operations; tag values are case-sensitive.
Not every resource type supports tags, and some (classic resources) cannot be tagged.

theory.heading: Tags are not inherited
theory.body: A tag on a resource group is not copied to the resources inside it. This surprises many people when a cost report grouped by tag shows a large 'untagged' slice. The fix is Azure Policy: built-in definitions such as 'Require a tag on resources' block untagged deployments, and 'Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing' uses the Modify effect to copy the tag automatically, with a remediation task for existing resources.
points: Require: use a Deny policy so untagged resources cannot be created.
Inherit: use a Modify policy with a managed identity and run remediation for existing resources.
Cost Management can also apply tag inheritance for cost data only, without changing resources.

theory.heading: Resource locks
theory.body: A lock overrides permissions: even an Owner cannot delete a resource with a CanNotDelete lock until the lock is removed. That extra deliberate step is the point; it stops a mistyped 'az group delete' from destroying production. Locks can be applied at subscription, resource group or resource scope and are inherited by all child resources. When different locks apply, the most restrictive one wins.
points: CanNotDelete (portal: Delete): users can read and modify but not delete.
ReadOnly (portal: Read-only): users can read but not modify or delete.
Locks apply to control-plane operations sent to management.azure.com.
Creating or deleting locks requires Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions, held by Owner and User Access Administrator.

theory.heading: Side effects of ReadOnly locks
theory.body: Because ReadOnly blocks any POST or PUT on the management plane, some apparently harmless actions fail. Listing storage account keys is a POST operation, so a ReadOnly lock can break tools that connect with keys. A ReadOnly lock on a resource group prevents adding new resources to it, and on App Service it can block Visual Studio Server Explorer and scaling. Prefer CanNotDelete unless you truly want a resource frozen.

lesson.title: Azure Management Tools: Portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and PowerShell
objectives: Compare the Azure portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell and know when to use each.
Translate common tasks between az commands and Az PowerShell cmdlets.
Filter and format CLI output with --query (JMESPath) and --output.
Explain how Cloud Shell authenticates and persists files.
Write a small, repeatable script instead of clicking through the portal.
lesson.definition: Azure offers several front ends to the same Azure Resource Manager API: the web-based Azure portal, the cross-platform Azure CLI (az commands), the Azure PowerShell Az module (Verb-AzNoun cmdlets) and Azure Cloud Shell, a browser-based shell with both tools pre-installed and already signed in. Because they all call ARM, anything created with one can be managed with another.

theory.heading: The Azure portal
theory.body: The portal at portal.azure.com is the best place to explore a service, see dashboards and understand options, and it is used heavily in the AZ-104 exam's scenario questions. It is a poor tool for repeatable work: clicking through 20 blades to build a lab cannot be reviewed, version-controlled or rerun. Many blades offer an 'Export template' or 'Download a template for automation' link, which is a useful bridge to infrastructure as code.
points: Good for discovery, one-off changes, dashboards and viewing metrics.
Supports custom dashboards and Azure Advisor recommendations.
Every portal action is recorded in the Activity Log like any other ARM call.

theory.heading: Azure CLI
theory.body: Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool written in Python, installed on Windows, macOS and Linux. Commands follow 'az <group> <subgroup> <action>', for example 'az vm create'. Output is JSON by default; '--output table' or '-o tsv' make it readable or script-friendly, and '--query' applies a JMESPath expression to pick fields. CLI scripts fit naturally in Bash and in CI/CD pipelines.
points: Sign in: az login; choose subscription: az account set --subscription <name>.
Output formats: json, jsonc, table, tsv, yaml, none.
JMESPath example: --query "[?powerState=='VM running'].name".
Use 'az <command> --help' and 'az find' to discover syntax.

theory.heading: Azure PowerShell
theory.body: The Az PowerShell module provides cmdlets named Verb-AzNoun, such as New-AzResourceGroup and Get-AzVM. PowerShell returns .NET objects rather than text, so you can pipe objects into Where-Object or Select-Object without parsing. It is popular with Windows administrators and in Azure Automation runbooks. The older AzureRM module is retired; use Az.
points: Sign in: Connect-AzAccount; choose subscription: Set-AzContext -Subscription <name>.
Objects, not strings: Get-AzVM | Where-Object Location -eq 'centralindia'.
Runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and cross-platform PowerShell 7.

theory.heading: Azure Cloud Shell
theory.body: Cloud Shell is a browser-based terminal available from the portal, shell.azure.com, the mobile app and VS Code. It offers Bash or PowerShell, includes Azure CLI, Az PowerShell, Terraform, kubectl, git and editors, and signs you in automatically with your portal identity. Sessions can be ephemeral, or you can mount an Azure file share so that files in your home directory persist between sessions. Sessions time out after about 20 minutes without interaction.
points: No local installation and always up-to-date tools.
Persistent storage uses an Azure Files share in a storage account you choose.
Runs as you: it has exactly your RBAC permissions, no more.
Can be deployed into a virtual network to reach private resources.

theory.heading: Choosing the right tool
theory.body: Use the portal to learn and to inspect; use CLI or PowerShell for repeatable tasks and bulk changes; use ARM templates or Bicep for whole environments. Scripts should be idempotent where possible: running 'az group create' twice simply returns the existing group, but other commands fail if the resource exists, so scripts often check first.
points: One-off investigation: portal.
Bulk or repeatable operations: CLI or PowerShell scripts.
Full environments under version control: Bicep or ARM templates (Day 19).
Scheduled operational tasks: Azure Automation runbooks or Functions.

# Azure PowerShell
New-AzResourceGroup -Name rg-lab-dev -Location centralindia
Get-AzVM -ResourceGroupName rg-lab-dev -Status |
  Where-Object PowerState -eq 'VM running' |
  Select-Object Name, @{n='Size';e={$_.HardwareProfile.VmSize}}

Cloud Shell is pre-authenticated, browser-based and can persist files on an Azure file share.

interview.question: What tools can you use to manage Azure resources?
interview.answer: The Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Cloud Shell, REST APIs and SDKs, and infrastructure-as-code tools such as ARM templates, Bicep and Terraform. All of them go through Azure Resource Manager.

interview.question: When would you prefer Azure CLI or PowerShell over the portal?
interview.answer: For repeatable, bulk or scheduled tasks, for anything that should be reviewed and version-controlled, and in pipelines. The portal is better for exploration and one-off checks.

interview.question: How does Cloud Shell store files between sessions?

interview.question: What is the key difference in how CLI and PowerShell return results?

interview.explanation: This explains why teams choose one or the other and why mixing them in one script is awkward.

practice.title: Script a reusable lab environment
practice.objective: Replace a sequence of portal clicks with a repeatable script and its PowerShell equivalent.
practice.statement: Your trainer creates the same lab for every batch: a resource group rg-az104-lab in Central India tagged env=lab and owner=<your email>, a general-purpose v2 storage account with locally redundant storage, and a CanNotDelete lock on the group. Write an Azure CLI script that builds it, a query that proves it exists, and the PowerShell equivalent of the resource group and lock steps. Finally, write the single command that removes everything at the end of the batch and explain why it fails until the lock is removed.

steps: Select the correct subscription with az account set.
Create the resource group with location and tags.
Create a StorageV2 account with Standard_LRS, using a globally unique lowercase name.
Create a CanNotDelete lock on the resource group.
Verify with az resource list and a --query that prints name and type as a table.
Write the PowerShell equivalents of the group and lock commands.
Write the clean-up commands in the correct order.
checklist: Storage account name is 3-24 lowercase letters and numbers only.
Tags use the key=value syntax in CLI and a hashtable in PowerShell.
The lock is removed before the resource group is deleted.
The script can be rerun without changing the result for the group creation step.
The verification query returns readable output, not raw JSON.
practice.sample_answer:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
az account set --subscription "AZ104-Training"
RG=rg-az104-lab; LOC=centralindia
az group create -n $RG -l $LOC --tags env=lab owner=student@example.com
az storage account create -n stlab$RANDOM$RANDOM -g $RG -l $LOC --kind StorageV2 --sku Standard_LRS
az lock create -n lock-lab --lock-type CanNotDelete -g $RG
az resource list -g $RG --query "[].{name:name,type:type}" -o table

# PowerShell equivalents
New-AzResourceGroup -Name rg-az104-lab -Location centralindia -Tag @{env='lab'; owner='student@example.com'}
New-AzResourceLock -LockName lock-lab -LockLevel CanNotDelete -ResourceGroupName rg-az104-lab

# Clean-up
az lock delete -n lock-lab -g $RG
az group delete -n $RG --yes --no-wait

Note: 'az group delete' alone fails with ScopeLocked because the CanNotDelete lock overrides RBAC; deleting the lock first is a deliberate second step. $RANDOM keeps the storage name unique, and 'az group create' is idempotent, so rerunning it updates rather than fails.

questions.answer: A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacentres. A region pair links two regions in the same geography for disaster recovery, staggered updates and prioritised recovery.

days.title: Azure Resource Manager: Management Groups, Subscriptions and Resource Groups
days.focus: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service for Azure: every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs or templates is authenticated, authorised and then sent by ARM to the right resource provider. ARM organises resources in a hierarchy of management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources, and access control, policy and budgets applied at one level are inherited by everything beneath it.
objectives: Explain what Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is and why every tool goes through it.

days.title: Tags and Resource Locks for Organising and Protecting Resources
days.focus: Tags are name-value pairs attached to Azure resources, resource groups and subscriptions to add metadata such as cost centre, environment or owner. Resource locks are management-plane safeguards that prevent accidental deletion (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly) to a scope and everything beneath it, regardless of the user's RBAC role.

Explain why tags are not inherited and how to enforce or inherit them with Azure Policy.
Compare CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks and predict which operations each blocks.

A lock on a scope applies to that scope and every path beneath it (whole segments only: a lock on 'sub1/rg' does not apply to 'sub1/rg-web'). Lock types are CanNotDelete (blocks delete) and ReadOnly (blocks write and delete). Reads are never blocked. For each operation, find all locks that apply; if any of them blocks the operation, print 'BLOCKED by <type> at <scope>' choosing ReadOnly before CanNotDelete and, among locks of the same type, the one closest to the top (fewest segments). Otherwise print 'ALLOWED'.

revision: Tags are name-value metadata used for cost, ownership and automation.
Tags are not inherited; use Azure Policy (Deny or Modify) to require or inherit them.
CanNotDelete allows modify but blocks delete; ReadOnly blocks modify and delete.
Locks are inherited by child scopes and override RBAC, even for Owners.
Only roles with Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* (Owner, User Access Administrator) manage locks.
ReadOnly locks can break operations that use POST, such as listing storage keys.

days.title: Azure Management Tools: Portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and PowerShell
days.focus: Azure offers several front ends to the same Azure Resource Manager API: the web-based Azure portal, the cross-platform Azure CLI (az commands), the Azure PowerShell Az module (Verb-AzNoun cmdlets) and Azure Cloud Shell, a browser-based shell with both tools pre-installed and already signed in. objectives: Compare the Azure portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell and know when to use each.
Translate common tasks between az commands and Az PowerShell cmdlets.
Filter and format CLI output with --query (JMESPath) and --output.

days.assignment: Your trainer creates the same lab for every batch: a resource group rg-az104-lab in Central India tagged env=lab and owner=<your email>, a general-purpose v2 storage account with locally redundant storage, and a CanNotDelete lock on the group. Write an Azure CLI script that builds it, a query that proves it exists, and the PowerShell equivalent of the resource group and lock steps. Finally, write the single command that removes everything at the end of the batch and explain why it fails until the lock is removed.
steps: Select the correct subscription with az account set.
Create the resource group with location and tags.
Create a StorageV2 account with Standard_LRS, using a globally unique lowercase name.
Create a CanNotDelete lock on the resource group.
Verify with az resource list and a --query that prints name and type as a table.
Write the PowerShell equivalents of the group and lock commands.
Write the clean-up commands in the correct order.
revision: Portal, CLI, PowerShell and Cloud Shell all call the same Azure Resource Manager API.
Azure CLI uses az <group> <action>; filter with --query (JMESPath) and format with -o.
Az PowerShell uses Verb-AzNoun cmdlets and returns objects you can pipe.
Cloud Shell is pre-authenticated, browser-based and can persist files on an Azure file share.
